posts.text: But how is shipping chips to China keeping the US ahead if they’re bottlenecked on compute?
No, no. We've got Vera Rubin for the United States. We have Vera Rubin for the United States. Now, am I in the United States? Do you consider me part of the United States?

You consider Nvidia a United States company? Okay. Number one, why is it that we don't come up with a regulation that's more balanced so that Nvidia can win around the world instead of giving up the world? Why would you want the United States to give up the world? The chip industry is part of the American ecosystem. It's part of American technology leadership. It's part of the AI ecosystem. It's part of AI leadership. Why is it that your policy, your philosophy, leads to the United States giving up a vast part of the world's market?

I guess the claim here is… Dario had this quote where he said that it's like Boeing bragging that we're selling North Korea nukes, but the missile casings are made by Boeing. And that's somehow enabling the US technology stack. Fundamentally, you're giving them this capability.
Comparing AI to anything that you just mentioned is lunacy.
But AI is similar to enriched uranium, right? It can have positive uses, it can have negative uses. We still don't want to send enriched uranium to other countries.
The analogy is that enriched uranium is like compute.
It's a lousy analogy. It's an illogical analogy.
But if that compute can run a model that can do zero-day exploits against all American software, how is that not a weapon?

First of all, the way to solve that problem is to have dialogues with the researchers and dialogues with China, and dialogues with all the countries to make sure that people don't use technology in that way. That's a dialogue that has to happen. Okay? Number one. Number two, we also need to make sure that the United States is ahead, that Vera Rubin, Blackwell, is available in the United States in abundance, mountains of it. Obviously, our results would show it. Abundance, tons of it. The amount of computing we have is great. We have amazing AI researchers here. It's great. We ought to stay ahead. However, we also have to recognize that AI is not just a model. AI is a five-layer cake. The AI industry matters across every single layer, and we want the United States to win at every single layer, including the chip layer. Conceding the entire market is not going to allow the United States to win the technology race long-term in the chip layer, in the computing stack. That is just a fact.

I guess then the crux comes down to, how does selling them chips now help us win in the long term? Tesla sold extremely good electric vehicles to China for a long time. iPhones are sold in China, extremely good. They didn't cause them lock-in. China will still make their version of EVs and they're dominating. Their smartphones are dominating.

When we started the conversation today, you acknowledged that Nvidia's position is very different. You used words like moat. The single most important thing to our company is the richness of our ecosystem, which is about developers. 50% of the AI developers are in China. The United States should not give that up.

But we have a lot of Nvidia developers in the US, and that doesn't prevent American labs from also being able to use other accelerators in the future. In fact, right now they're using other accelerators as well, which is fine and great. I don't see why that wouldn't be the case in China as well, if you sell them Nvidia chips, just the same way that Google can use TPUs and Nvidia—

We have to keep innovating and, as you probably know, our share is growing, not decreasing. The premise that even if we competed in China, that we're going to lose that market anyways… You're not talking to somebody who woke up a loser. That loser attitude, that loser premise makes no sense to me. We're not a car. We are not a car. The fact that I can buy this car brand one day and use another car brand another day, easy. Computing is not like that. There's a reason why the x86 deal exists. There's a reason why ARM is so sticky. These ecosystems are hard to replace. It costs an enormous amount of time and energy, and most people don't want to do it. So it's our job to continue to nurture that ecosystem, to keep advancing the technology so that we can compete in the marketplace. Conceding a marketplace based on the premise you described, I simply can't acknowledge that. It makes no sense. Because I don't think the United States is a loser. Our industry is not a loser. That losing proposition, that losing mindset, makes no sense to me.
Okay. I'll move on. I just want to make sure that—
You don't have to move on. I'm enjoying it.
Okay, great. Then I won't. I appreciate that. But I think maybe the crux… and thanks for walking around the circles with me, because I think it helps bring out what the crux here is.
The crux is you're going to extremes. Your argument starts from extremes. That if we give them any compute at all in this narrow moment, we will lose everything.
No, I think what my argument is—

Let me just make my argument for myself. The idea is not that there is some key threshold of compute. It's that any marginal compute is helpful. So if you have more compute, you can train a better model.
And I just want you to acknowledge that any marginal sales for the American technology industry is beneficial.

I actually don't… If the AI models that run on those chips are capable of cyber offensive capabilities, or the chips are training models with cyber capabilities and running more instances of those models, it is not a nuclear weapon, but it enables a weapon of a kind.
The logic that you use, you might as well say it to microprocessors and DRAMs. You might as well say it to electricity.
But in fact we do have export controls on the technology that is relevant to making the most advanced DRAM. We have all kinds of export controls on China for all kinds of chip-making stuff.
We sell a lot of DRAM and CPUs into China, and I think it's right.

I guess this goes back to the fundamental question of, is AI different? If you have the kind of technology where they can find these zero-days in software, is that something where we want to minimize China's ability to get there first, to deploy it widely?
We want the United States to be ahead. We can control that.
How do we control that if the chips are already there and they're using them to train that model?
We have tons of compute. We have tons of AI researchers. We're racing as fast as we can.
Again, we have more nuclear weapons than anybody else, but we don't want to send enriched uranium anywhere.
We're not enriched uranium. It's a chip, and it's a chip that they can make themselves.
But there's a reason they're buying it from you. We have quotes from the founders of Chinese companies that say that they’re bottlenecked on compute.

Because our chips are better. On balance, our chips are better. There's just no question about it. In the absence of our chip… Can you acknowledge that Huawei had a record year? Can you acknowledge that a whole bunch of chip companies have gone public? Can you acknowledge that?

Can you also acknowledge that we used to have a very large share in that market, and we no longer have a large share in that market? We can also acknowledge that China is about 40% of the world's technology industry. To concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country. It is a disservice to our national security. It is a disservice to our technology leadership, all for the benefit of one company. It makes no sense to me.
The elephant in the room here is the race with China. H
the argument has been we can't slow down AI progress lest we lose to China.
Do you think that's a valid argument?

Um as an advice to every single CEO in every industry, every student, every professor, every member of the American society, we want America to be as prosperous as we can. The more prosperous we are, the richer we are as an economy, the more we could provide for social security, the more we could provide for national military security, the the better we could be a citizen of the world and support other people's challenges and trials and tribulation and pain and suffering, um the more philanthropic we can be as a nation. And so I would advise that every single American citizen, everybody in America pulls in the same direction as hard as we can.
So should we slow down and would that affect the race with China? The American standing in

we should go as fast as we can irrespective of anybody else. It's not um if China were to discover a cure for cancer, it's great for us. If China were to uh invent a new technology for sustainable energy, it's great for us. If China were to uh uh lead in many areas of science and math and we were able to learn from them and benefit from it, it's great for us. But listen, we're packing heat as a nation. This is a nation with extraordinary capability, extraordinary innovators. I'm proud to be part of the American technology industry that I would consider one of the three pillars of our national treasures. Of course, our financial system is one of them. Of course, our military is one of them. You know, the the the the industry that I serve, that I'm part of, the technology industry is absolutely one of our national treasures. We are going to go as fast as we can, but

how important is it? We're going to go as fast as we can, but we would never ever and never should ship products before they're ready, deliver products that are unsafe, and nobody's expecting us to do that. But everybody's expecting us to succeed and help America be as prosperous as possible.

David Saxs told me earlier this week that he believes that if we slow down the rate of AI development, then that could do huge damage to the American economy, the American military and put the United States at a disadvantage. So I just want to clearly understand like do you think that we should be pacing the development of AI right now given where we are visav China?

First of all, David is incredibly smart. Um, this is thoughtful. He's deep. He's pragmatic. Um, he is he is one of the one of the great American patriots. Um, it's been a privilege to to know him and um I met him when he was an adviser at the White House and um uh incredible incredible human. Um, I'm not exactly what what the context of what he said was, uh, but I'm fairly certain he wants America to go as fast as we can, but not faster than we should. We should go as fast as we can, but not faster than we should. And if we're if we're compromising safety, that can't happen. Um, if you're compromising safety and you deliver products that are unsafe, that put people in harm's way, we have laws of all kinds to come after you. And so the companies that are developing these technologies are perfectly incentivized to do the right thing. And I have every confidence. I have every confidence because they're incentivized to do so. They have the capability to do so. that we will deliver, we will create AI, advance AI in a way that's safe to society.
Dario Amade says we should stop selling chips to China. The quote is do not sell powerful AI chips or semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China. What's your response to that?

Well, um we have to we have to make sure that that uh technology that's created by America advantage America first. Every country would do that. Every company does that. Every parent does that. Every company does that. Every industry does that. Every nation does that. And in the case of in the case of the American America has decided, the United States has decided and and I'm very supportive that we provide Nvidia's best technology to American companies first. And so we're in the generation of what we call Vera Rubin. Vera Rubin is shipping in volume production. Um we are several years ahead of China with this technology and um it's being made available to uh to Dario and uh Sam and you know the American labs and uh American industries and that's exactly what we're doing and we're we're delighted to do that. Um on the other hand remember that AI is a five layer cake. It is not just that model. The AI industry represent is represented by the energy sector, the chips sector, the model sector where where they are, the model layer where they are. Um, you could argue that there's six layers or five, but above that is basically the data and the application layer. And we need every single one of these layers, everybody in America to win. We want us to win in the energy sector. We'd like us to lead the world in the chip sector. Uh, we like to make sure that every single application company I love the fact that FedEx is going to be an AI company. I love the fact that Walmart's going to be an AI company. We need every single company in America to be an AI company. Not just one company, not just two companies. Remember, you got to take a step back and remember what what AI is. AI is intell digital intelligence. Why is it how is it possible that every single company in America is not supported and have capabilities of digital intelligence? And so of course every company is going to be a company of the future with digital intelligence or artificial intelligence as part of the company. And so I want everybody to win including the chips industry. And so,
so you disagree with Daario's position that we should not sell?

I completely disagree that uh we should ban China of all American products. The American company should have advanced capabilities. But then after that, every single layer of the American AI tech stack, including the traditional companies and the AI model companies of every single field and every single chip company should go and serve the world, compete for the world. Serving the world, having market have capturing market share, capturing economic prosperity, that's all about competing. America is about competition and we ought to go and compete and not seed entire markets. Our our market is not his to seed. Our market is not his to seed. We ought to go compete for the world's market.
I have two just quick questions for you here. Um you will be attending the state dinner with President Xiinping of China. Is that correct? Next week.
if you get a chance to speak to him about this situation that we're in right now, the one that Americans are so concerned about, what will you say to the president of China?

Um, I would I would say that that um I'm delighted to see uh AI's technology transitioning from from laboratories to now really useful capabilities and products and services. And because it's making that transition, it would be good for um all countries that are developing and advancing AI to do so in a way where we share best practices. Um maybe maybe set um uh global standards about uh product expectations.

Work Yeah, of course. Yeah, of course. Work closer together. Um I if we want look they want China to be safe. They want China to have the benefit of AI. They want China to prosper just as we want United States to prosper. I'm glad they have ambitious expectations and aspirations. I want I wish every country Don't you wish every country has aspirations and ambitions for a better tomorrow? And I love that about them. Um, as they advance the technology, uh, we ought to make sure that we work with each other as much as we can, as much as we can. There are, of course, areas where we we can't work together for whatever reason. Um, maybe it's militarily, well, it could be military reasons. It could be um other national security reasons that that that um could arise. And uh, and those are those are for for the governments to sort out. Other than that, I think that it would be great for us to work in every possible way.

Jensen Huang out at Nvidia. He resigned before he was fired being replaced by the CFO of that company, Colette Kress. Interesting, they went with a woman actually. So and I think she's seen as like an interim chief, not a permanent replacement. In any case, joining us now to break down what all of this means is Garrison Lovely. He is the author of Obsolete: The AI Industry's Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us and How to Stop It. Great to see you, Garrison. Welcome.

Yeah, so your reaction to this news. I was just looking it looks like Nvidia's stock has dropped another 10%. Markets overall not doing great, but not like a total catastrophe. It's mostly been primarily focused on Nvidia here. What the hell happened and what is it going to mean?

Truly one of the wildest stories of all time. So what we've what we have here is that Jensen Huang has been selling over $7 billion of AI chips to a network of fraudulent smuggling companies [laughter] that were tied to a suspected Chinese spy while successfully lobbying the US government and Trump to make it easier to sell chips to Chinese companies. And Trump learned about all of this and then let Jensen come with him to China and did just continued letting this other company buy all these chips. And it's just hard to overstate how significant this is. It's the scandal of the century.

And can you tell us a little bit about how important Jensen Huang is to the AI industry, not just as a business leader, as a thinker, as somebody who pushed the acceleration button on this successfully, of course, with the Trump administration, which has had a great relationship with him as much of this has accelerated, but he is really baked fundamentally into the cake first of all of the stock market right now of the American economy and the entire AI industry because the chips are so essential to progress for American AI companies. Tell us a little bit about how inextricably intertwined, at least until now, he was with the entire AI economy.

Yeah, until this happened, Jensen Huang was the most powerful man in AI because he built Nvidia. He is synonymous with the company. And Nvidia ships from the very beginning of the deep learning revolution back in 2012 were the best way to train and run these large language models and deep learning models in general. And he has there's way more demand for these chips than their supply. So Jensen was personally deciding who got which chips when, which could determine whether your company lived or died. And so this has massive implications for the entire industry. Nvidia still has a ton of I mean all the same researchers and engineers besides Jensen and will still be formidable in developing the most advanced chips in the world. But the way Jensen just decided this stuff and the way he was able to push the administration to loosen these these restrictions on chip sales which unique to him and now everything touching him and everything close to him has been discredited including these arguments around we need to sell more chips to China to beat China and also beating China is really important to us and it's like is it? [laughter] You know, it just calls into question everything that's being pushed by the accelerationist deregulatory right.

Um let me go ahead and play for you just to underscore how close this relationship with Jensen and Trump was, is, etc. I mean Trump was defending him right up to the last moment. What took him out, I mentioned this before but just to reiterate for people, is another affair was revealed. This one doesn't appear to have been with the spy but was with another Nvidia executive which poses its own problems and I think there was a sense of okay well if there's you know the famous tweet if there's two ants in the kitchen that you see you don't have a two ant problem. Um so I think there was a sense of where is the bottom going to be on this and especially if more details as more details came out about how likely it was they knew about this smuggling operation, whether the woman involved was really a Chinese spy or not. In any case, let's play C6 here guys. This Trump calling Jensen while he's on stage at the all-in summit in the wake of the hugging face incident when there was a massively heightened concern about the continued rollout and training and development of AI models. Let's go ahead and take a listen to that.
Mr. President, you're you're now talking to the planet.

The great thing about life is Jensen can develop the most complex computer chip in the world that nobody can copy for 10 years, but he can't figure out how to hook me on speaker phone. And I'm telling you it's all a hoax. The data centers are great and they make people wealthy and they make states wealthy and it's the oil of the next 20 25 years. It's bigger than the internet and the AI, you know, much more so. And they're just playing right into the hands of a lot of people that don't want to see it happen and that could be political people and it could also be China. And we're not going to let that happen. It's a it's a hoax. And
You're right. We're not going to let that happen, sir.

So this was a very close relationship between Jensen and Trump. He was between him and David Sachs probably the two most influential policy advisors with regard to AI visa vis the president. What do we know Garrison specifically about when Trump knew about both the, you know, alleged Chinese spy aspect, the fact that the alleged Chinese spy was running this apparent smuggling operation? How do all of those pieces fit together? Because to me that's one of the wildest parts of this story.

Yeah. So Trump was first briefed in October 2025 that Alice Wong and Jensen Wong had a relationship and was presumed to be a spy. And when Trump was going to take Jensen with him to China, I think in October, Marco Rubio reminded him of this fact. They decided not to take Jensen, changed his mind and then picked Jensen up in Alaska, brought him with him to China.

And with respect to the smuggling, the New York Times reported this months ago as a possibility. And Mega Speed, the main company Alice Wong was associated with, like didn't have a real headquarters. You know, the address was like not it went to some place that was clearly a front. And it was buying 4 and 1/2 billion dollars of Nvidia chips and was the top customer in all of Southeast Asia. And Southeast Asia is one of the biggest regions in the world for AI computing power uh because so many companies in China have headquarters in Singapore or are doing remote compute from Southeast Asian countries. Like these are not super wealthy countries. They can't afford to buy billions and billions of dollars of these ships. And it's just pretty obvious from looking into this at all and like short sellers even noticed this months ago as well that these are not legit companies and the fact that they got all these ships seems entirely a result of Jensen's relationship with this woman. And she herself was touting it in her communications. She was posting WeChat photos of them together publicly. Uh this is why, you know, short sellers were able to figure out what was going on well before, you know, it was reported in the news and uh it it just really was not it was kind of an open secret and these rumors were going around for for ever. And Jensen has consistently said there's no smuggling. There's no evidence of chip diversions. And that's clearly now, right? And it was at the time to anybody who knew anything about this. And I think that is like the piece that could be easily missed is that, you know, this was an effectively criminal operation that was being covered up by Nvidia. Nvidia was also under reporting the number of chips sold to these companies to the US government. So misrepresenting material information to the US government. And the fact that Trump is just fine with all this is I mean even for him [laughter] is pretty amazing.
Well, now they've elevated the CFO. I mean, if they're cooking the books in terms of what they're reporting, that person seems like they would be potentially implicated here too, Garrison.

It's it's totally possible. I mean, the general counsel Tim Teeter is the person who I've seen invoked in uh other situations, I should say. Um and there's been reporting where he squashed a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed.

Well, so yeah, the the fact that the the sales actually went through was the one thing that gives me pause and the kind of obvious explanation that this was controlled espionage, counter espionage that the government confronted Jensen Huang said, listen, you're in a relationship with a Chinese spy because why wouldn't they if they knew? And then uh we're sort of managing the relationship and using it to glean uh any information that they could and he became an asset, something like that, which would seem a fairly obvious explanation, but the sales went through. So that's kind of an interesting part of all of this, Garrison. We don't talk enough about the possibility that these massively powerful AI companies are swamped with espionage. We talked about it a little bit with OpenAI recently. Can you just speak to, you know, from studying these companies, how vulnerable they are, how prolific espionage might be? What do you know about all this?
Yeah, I mean, the context here is that this is the first [snorts] incredibly consequential general purpose technology with national security implications being developed in the private sector.

And so the Manhattan Project was, you know, secret and they were all in the desert together. That was still infiltrated by the Soviets and Stalin knew more about the bomb than Harry Truman. These companies are headquartered in San Francisco. They have terrible information security practices and cybersecurity practices. And the idea that, you know, they're able to keep any of these important secrets from China or other state actors is laughable and everyone in the industry kind of understands this. And apparently like I've I've heard from people that, you know, CEOs also understand this. And and Dario Amodei has said publicly, you know, if China wanted to get our model weights, they they could do that. And so it it really makes all of this look so ridiculous. It's like they're racing as fast as possible to develop the most capable models and to learn the secrets of how to build them, but they have no way of keeping their secrets secret. And then Nvidia has been pushing to allow China access to more chips, which chips are the only thing that you can really control. Uh you know, the information about how to train these models is just so easy to leak. People can learn it and just go to work at another company. But the chips are, you know, the thing that really can determine who has the best models. And you know, my position is that we should not be racing to build these labor replacing machines because it's undemocratic and dangerous. But if your position is that the United States needs to stay ahead of China, then letting them have access to these chips while also letting these companies run such a loose ship is just a completely incoherent mess. And now we're seeing it's downstream of uh corruption and a Chinese spy uh affair and just like kind of puts the lie to the whole thing.

Yeah. I mean, one of the takes that I've seen that I think is probably right is that there's a reason why this information is being really pushed forward now right after the election too. Trump takes this big drubbing. He's seen as a little weaker. Democrats are coming into power. Marco Rubio or whoever, you know, takes this to the press and they're able to to push out this story that this woman is an alleged Chinese spy. I've seen some push back on the idea that she is a spy. To me, that part is not the most important question, although I will say she's back in Beijing now, which to me sort of lends credence to the spy idea, but I don't really know. Um to me, the bigger piece is the smuggling operation, the fact that this was clearly happening. The White House knew about it. Nvidia knew about it. Jensen knew about it and no one did anything about it. However you feel about the underlying issue, that is a criminal act. Um and I agree with you, Garrison. I'm not a China hawk by any mean. I that means I think we should be, you know, collaborating with China. I don't think we should do be doing a trade war with China. However, I am against the further development of these models period. So, whether it's the American companies or the Chinese companies, so that's why I think a restriction on these these chips and control over them is important. But what do you make of that piece of of this is sort of like a deep state plot against Jensen and that's why we should go out and defend him.

So Jensen, David Sachs, Howard Lutnick, those three men have been pushing the administration to loosen these chip restrictions. And almost everyone else in the administration from reporting we've seen have been in favor of tightening the restrictions. And so there's a lot of people who wanted to break up Jensen and Trump and also have bones to pick with Lutnick. And Nvidia, the way they've been lobbying in DC is incredibly aggressive. Just like unheard of levels of intimidation trying to get think tank researchers fired for criticizing Nvidia or for promoting export controls. And when I've been doing reporting and talking to people who work on these chip restrictions, they don't want to say anything on the record about Nvidia. But the moment we go off the record or on background, it's the first thing they want to talk about. And [snorts] so now that Nvidia is in this weakened position, now that Jensen is out and presumably people who are close to him will also go down for this, there's the floodgates are starting to open and people want to tell these stories. And you know, in in my book I argue for a bilateral deal with the US and China to stop building these AI models that are designed to replace us. And I was uncertain about how to feel about the export controls overall because they do increase the kind of race tensions and the aggressive, you know, posture between the countries. But if you think about what a deal banning development of the most capable models will look like, it's going to involve restrictions on computing power and like export controls plus plus plus.

And so if you can't even get export controls that most people in DC think are good because Nvidia is fighting them so hard, then you're not going to be able to get to a much much harder endgame. And so I see this as a a really positive development for people who want an end to this race.

That's interesting. We have to ask you about the Howard Lutnick of it all. Axios had a report yesterday we can toss up on the screen. This is C5 saying that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over a failure to place Nvidia customer MegaSpeed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns. Sources familiar told Axios, they further reported at a situation room meeting on Thursday after the midterm elections, Bessent pressed Lutnick on why MegaSpeed had not been added to the Commerce Department's entity list to which Lutnick responded he would quote look into it. Commerce Under Secretary Jeff Kessler was also repeatedly also was repeatedly warned about MegaSpeed in deputy meetings. Kessler deferred to Lutnick saying that's a decision for the secretary, throwing the secretary under the bus. Sources told Axios that Lutnick has spent the last year quote unquote undoing efforts by other administration officials to hold MegaSpeed, a company accused as we were talking about of illegally diverting US trips to China accountable because of concerns it would escalate the trade war with China. Now, Garrison, interestingly, Howard Lutnick's former company is does a decent bit of business in terms of data centers, real estate and data centers. So I have no idea if that had anything to do with this. His his family
that company does, yeah. It's controlled by his son and Lutnick doesn't, you know, own any of it anymore, but has hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia positions as of a few months ago.

Isn't that interesting? Yeah, tell us what you're reading into this and if it suggests that right now there's going to be a kind of I don't know, the the dynamics of the Trump administration are kind of weirdly split on this because you have some absolute accelerationists like Jensen in Trump's ear and then you have China hawks like Bessent in Trump's ear. So what are you reading into the dynamics, Garrison?

the first thing is they have still not put MegaSpeed on the blacklist. This is a company tied to this suspected spy that is clearly just smuggling these chips. And that's just mind-boggling. Like truly. Like before it's public, it's like maybe there's some case we're keeping under wraps. But we've also just learned today that Singapore held Alice Wong, the suspected spy earlier this year for I think months. And the US did not speak with her apparently and just seemed not interested in this. So it's it's really really wild. Um and that Axios report, you know, the the level of detail in there is really impressive reporting and kind of speaks to the frustration and and anger towards Luttig from other members of the administration to be giving like every detail of all of this. And yeah, it it seems to be Luttig versus all the other cabinet secretaries standing alone with David Sachs, who's not in the admin anymore, but was very influential and and still is very influential with Trump as the former AI czar and Jensen, those three people were pushing loosening these restrictions. And the Commerce Department is responsible for enforcing them. And so you can have a rule, but if the people who are supposed to be enforcing it just aren't, then it doesn't really matter very much. And this is a problem for Congress going forward because they can legislate new restrictions and there's a bunch that are going into this must-pass defense authorization bill.
And they're likely to succeed much more so now that Jensen is been disgraced in this way. But it's the agency
going to be like a dog with a bone with you know, incoming likely chair of the Senate Banking Committee. Um she is already saying we are going to investigate what the hell is going on here.
Right right. But yeah, if the department and the agency responsible for enforcement just isn't doing it and the president is shielding the secretary, then it's like you're kind of in this standoff.

And you know, Luttig and Trump have known each other for 30 plus years. And Lutnick and Epstein were very close as well. And there's just a lot more going on here than we know about. And I think this scandal is going to keep growing and growing.

He denies that Garrison Lutnick says that the moment that he met Epstein [clears throat] he told his wife this is a disgusting man. I want nothing to do with him even before they went went to the island or whatever thing he did with them afterwards.
no he went to the island too.
Yeah with his daughters I believe if memory serves. Yeah okay. Anyway yeah who doesn't take their teenage daughters to Epstein Island.
There were a bunch of other teenage girls there.

Oh that makes it that makes it fine. Um Garrison last piece on this then I want to talk to you some about the the leadership fights um that are are relevant to AI deeply relevant to AI and what happens next. Just read a Chinese article calling this "the darkest moment for Chinese AI." Seeing pushback in the comments, but basically it lays out the bear case quite extensively:

1. Getting compute is harder whichever way you go. Buying advanced NVIDIA chips is difficult, renting GPUs overseas is coming under pressure, and proposed restrictions on chipmaking equipment could make domestic alternatives harder to produce too.

2. Catching up could get a lot more expensive. If learning from leading models’ outputs aka distillaion becomes harder, Chinese labs have to spend more on their own data, experiments and training. That gets uncomfortable if investors are also losing patience. Independent labs don’t have an advertising or e-commerce business to pay the bills.

3. Robot-brain startups could find their advantage disappearing. Frontier labs are moving into robotics, potentially eating into what specialist models can offer. Meanwhile, robots still have to make economic sense against China’s relatively low labor costs.

4. More users don’t necessarily mean enough revenue. China has huge digital audiences, but getting people and businesses to pay sustainably for AI is another question. Everyone is competing on price, American models are getting cheaper too, and research isn’t getting cheaper.

5. Even the areas where China already leads face risks. Optical-component suppliers are benefiting from AI infrastructure spending, but proposed US restrictions could threaten access to major customers.

That’s a lot hitting at once. The worry is that companies keep making better models while needing more money to stay competitive, without earning enough to fund the next round.

Now, it feels like every six months it is a "darkest moment" for Chinese AI. But I think these are real concerns. We'll focus on this topic at @techbuzzchina (and present some hope, I think) next week.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
